lessons.title: Lesson 1: What customer service work looks like with AI
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Describe customer service jobs and how AI tools are used in them.
This lesson builds toward: Given three customer service job posts, you will describe the main customer service jobs and how agents use AI tools such as chatbots, suggested replies and knowledge bases, naming at least one tool and one human task for each job.
Customer service agents help people by phone, chat, email, social media or in person. Common job titles: customer service representative, support agent, call center agent, help desk technician and client care specialist.
AI now handles many simple questions through chatbots, so human agents get the harder, more emotional or unusual cases. Agents often use AI tools that suggest replies, search the company's knowledge base, summarize long conversations and write ticket notes.
That makes human skills more valuable: listening, empathy, staying calm, judgment and solving problems. AI suggests; you decide what is right for the customer and follow company policy.
Words to know:
- Customer service representative: a person whose job is helping customers with questions and problems.
- Knowledge base: a company's library of answers and how-to articles.
- Ticket: a record of one customer issue and what was done about it.
Try it now: Look at three customer service job posts. Write down the job titles, whether they mention AI, chat or specific tools, and three skills each one asks for.
You can now describe customer service jobs and how agents use AI tools.

check.q: What does a human support agent usually handle when a company uses chatbots?
options: Only password resets
Nothing, because chatbots do all the work
Harder and more emotional cases
Only cases in another language
check.why: Chatbots take simple questions, so people get the harder cases that need care and judgment.

check.q: A job post asks for "experience with a ticketing system." You have never used one. What would you do?
options: Skip the job because you do not qualify
Apply and show related skills, and learn what a ticket system does
Say on your résumé that you used one
Ask a chatbot to apply for you
check.why: You can apply honestly, show related skills and learn the tool; lying on a résumé is never the answer.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The five-step customer contact
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Handle a customer contact from greeting to close using five steps.
This lesson builds toward: In a role-play with a customer, you will handle the contact from greeting to close using the five steps: greet, listen, confirm, solve and close, using all five steps in order.
Most good contacts follow five steps. Greet: say your name and offer help. Listen: let them explain without interrupting, and ask questions to understand. Confirm: repeat the problem back in your own words. Solve: give the answer or next steps, clearly. Close: check it is solved, ask if there is anything else, and thank them.
Example: "Thanks for calling, this is Dee. How can I help?" ... "So your order shows delivered but you didn't get it. Let me check." ... "I've sent a replacement; it arrives Thursday. Is there anything else I can help with?"
Verify identity using the company's process before sharing account details. Never ask for information the process does not require, and never ask for a full password.
Step by step:
- Greet with your name and an offer to help.
- Listen without interrupting; ask questions.
- Confirm the problem in your own words.
- Solve or explain next steps clearly.
- Close: check, ask if anything else, thank them.
Words to know:
- Verify identity: confirm the customer is who they say they are using the company's steps.
- Resolution: the solution to the customer's problem.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant: "Play a customer whose package says delivered but never arrived. Stay in character. After we finish, rate me on greet, listen, confirm, solve and close." Run the role-play.
You can now handle a customer contact from greeting to close using five steps.

check.q: Which step comes right after you greet the customer?
options: Solve
Close
Confirm
Listen
check.why: After the greeting you listen to the whole problem before you confirm or solve it.

check.q: You think the problem is solved. What would you do before ending the contact?
options: Check it is solved, ask if anything else is needed and thank them
Hang up quickly to take the next call
Tell them to call back if it breaks
Ask them to rate you five stars
check.why: A good close checks the fix, asks if anything else is needed and thanks the customer.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Calming an upset customer
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use de-escalation steps to calm an upset customer and find a solution.
This lesson builds toward: In a role-play with an upset customer, you will calm the customer with the HEAT steps and decide when to escalate, without arguing or saying "calm down".
Upset customers are usually upset at the situation, not at you. Stay calm, keep your voice low and slow, and do not argue or take it personally.
Use the HEAT steps: Hear them out, Empathize ("I understand how frustrating that is"), Apologize for the experience, and Take action (tell them exactly what you will do). Avoid "calm down" and "that's not my job".
Know your limits. If someone is abusive or threatening, follow your company's policy, which often allows a warning and then ending the contact, or handing it to a supervisor. Taking short breaks and talking with coworkers after hard calls helps you stay well.
Step by step:
- Stay calm and do not take it personally.
- Hear them out fully.
- Empathize and apologize for the experience.
- Take action: say exactly what you will do.
- If abusive, follow company policy or get a supervisor.
Words to know:
- De-escalation: calming a tense situation.
- Empathy: showing you understand how someone feels.
- Escalate: pass a case to a supervisor or specialist.
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant to play an angry customer whose bill was charged twice. Use HEAT. Then ask the AI which phrases worked and which to change.
You can now calm an upset customer with HEAT and know when to escalate.

check.q: What does the T in HEAT stand for?
options: Talk faster
Transfer
Take action
Thank
check.why: HEAT is Hear, Empathize, Apologize and Take action.

check.q: A customer is shouting about a double charge. What would you say first?
options: "I hear you, and I'm sorry this happened. Let me look at it now."
"Calm down so I can help you."
"That's not my department."
"You must have clicked twice."
check.why: Hearing and empathizing first lowers the heat; blaming or saying calm down raises it.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: AI tools and getting hired

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Using AI suggested replies and the knowledge base
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI suggestions as a starting point and check them before sending.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI-suggested reply, you will check the reply against the knowledge base and policy and edit it before sending, so every fact and promise matches policy.
Many support systems show AI-suggested replies or answers pulled from the knowledge base. They save time, but they can be wrong, out of date, or not fit this customer's situation.
Before you send: read it fully, check facts against the knowledge base or policy (dates, prices, refund rules), make it fit this person (use their name, answer what they asked), and fix the tone. If AI suggests something against policy, like a refund you are not allowed to give, do not send it.
To practice at home, paste a made-up customer message into a free AI assistant and ask: "Draft a friendly reply. Our policy: refunds within 30 days with receipt." Then edit it as if you were the agent.
Step by step:
- Read the suggested reply fully.
- Check facts against the knowledge base or policy.
- Personalize it for this customer.
- Fix the tone.
- Do not send anything against policy.
Words to know:
- Suggested reply: a reply drafted by AI that an agent can edit and send.
- Policy: the company's official rules.
Try it now: Write a made-up customer email about a late refund. Ask AI to draft a reply using a policy you make up, then edit it and mark every change you made.
You can now use AI-suggested replies safely by checking, personalizing and following policy.

options: A final answer you must send
A draft the AI writes that you check and edit
A message from your supervisor
A survey the customer fills in
check.why: The suggestion is only a starting point; you check it and decide what to send.

check.q: An AI draft promises a refund in two days, but policy says five to seven days. What would you do?
options: Send it because the AI wrote it
Delete the whole reply and send nothing
Change the timing to match policy before sending
Ask the customer which timing they prefer
check.why: Every fact and promise must match policy before you send.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Writing ticket notes and protecting customer data
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write clear ticket notes and handle customer information safely.
This lesson builds toward: After a customer contact, you will write ticket notes that record the issue, what you did, what was promised and the follow-up, with every required part and no passwords or private data.
Every contact needs notes so the next agent knows what happened. Good ticket notes are short and factual: the issue, what you checked, what you did, what was promised and any follow-up date. Example: "Customer reports missing package, order shows delivered 10/12. Checked carrier tracking. Sent replacement, arrives 10/16. Follow up if not received."
Some tools let AI summarize the conversation into notes. Check the summary: AI may miss a promise or add something that did not happen.
Protect data: only access accounts you are helping, never share customer details with anyone not allowed, never paste customer information into AI tools your company has not approved, and never write full card numbers or passwords in notes. Following privacy rules is part of the job.
Step by step:
- Write the issue in one line.
- Write what you checked and what you did.
- Write anything promised and the follow-up date.
- Check any AI summary for missing or wrong details.
- Leave out full card numbers and passwords.
Words to know:
- Ticket notes: a short written record of a customer contact.
- Data privacy: keeping people's personal information safe and only using it as allowed.
Try it now: Write ticket notes for the two role-plays you did in Chapter 1. Then ask AI to summarize one role-play and compare its summary with your notes.
You can now write clear ticket notes and protect customer information.

options: They let the next agent pick up the case without asking the customer again
They are only for the company's lawyers
They replace talking to the customer
They are a place to write your opinion of the customer
check.why: Clear notes let anyone continue the case without making the customer repeat everything.

check.q: A customer reads you their card number by mistake. What would you write in the notes?
options: The full card number so it is saved
The card number and their password
Nothing at all about the call
The issue and actions taken, with no card number
check.why: Notes record the issue and actions, never full card numbers or passwords.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Getting hired in customer service
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Show your customer service skills on a résumé and in an interview.
This lesson builds toward: Given a job post, you will write résumé bullets and a STAR interview answer that show your customer service skills, with three bullets and one complete STAR story.
Employers want reliability, a calm attitude, clear communication, basic computer skills and a willingness to learn. Experience from retail, food service, caregiving, church, the military or work inside all counts.
Write résumé bullets that show results: "Helped 60+ customers a day in a busy kitchen line with a calm, friendly attitude." Ask AI to help turn your experience into customer service bullets, and keep them true.
Expect role-play questions: "A customer is yelling about a late order. What do you do?" Answer with your steps (HEAT and the five-step contact). Prepare a STAR story about a time you calmed someone or solved a problem. Some employers give a typing or computer skills test, so practice typing with a free online typing test.
Step by step:
- List experience where you helped people.
- Ask AI to turn it into true résumé bullets with numbers.
- Prepare a STAR story about calming someone or solving a problem.
- Practice a role-play answer with HEAT.
- Practice typing with a free online typing test.
Words to know:
- Role-play question: an interview question where you show how you would handle a situation.
- Typing test: a test of how fast and accurately you type.
Try it now: Final task: role-play three customer contacts with AI (simple question, upset customer, problem not solved on first try), write ticket notes for each, then write three résumé bullets and a STAR answer about calming an upset customer.
You can now handle customers with AI tools like a support agent and show those skills to get hired.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Contact flow Skipped steps, such as solving before listening or ending without a close. Used greet, listen, confirm, solve and close in all three contacts. Also verified identity where needed and set a clear next step on the unsolved problem. Calming the upset customer Argued, blamed or said "calm down". Used Hear, Empathize, Apologize and Take action, and the customer calmed down. Also knew when to escalate and explained the next step clearly. AI checked Sent an AI suggestion that did not match policy. Checked every AI suggestion against the knowledge base or policy before using it. Can point to each change made and say why. Ticket notes Notes are missing the issue, actions, promise or follow-up, or include private data. Each ticket has the issue, what was done, what was promised and the follow-up, with no private data. Notes are short enough that another agent could continue without asking anything. Ready to get hired Bullets are vague, or the STAR answer is missing a part. Three clear résumé bullets and a STAR answer with all four parts. Bullets include numbers, and the STAR answer ends with a real result. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What does the R in a STAR answer stand for?
options: Reason
Reply
Rating
Result
check.why: STAR is Situation, Task, Action and Result.

check.q: You worked in a prison kitchen serving 200 people a day. How would you use it on a customer service résumé?
options: Leave it off because it does not count
Write a bullet about serving 200 people a day quickly and politely
Say only that you were busy
Describe it as a manager job
check.why: Real experience serving people counts; describe it honestly with a number.
